tagline.text: Where T'boli dreamweavers turn dreams into abaca cloth

location.label: Location
location.text: Lamdalag area, Lake Sebu, South Cotabato

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: Approx. ₱300–2,500 (depending on purchases; per person per day including transport)

children.text: T'nalak is an ikat cloth woven by T'boli women of Lake Sebu, South Cotabato, from abaca threads patterned with designs received in dreams. At the Lang Dulay Weaving Center and the School of Living Traditions you can meet the weavers at their looms.

T'nalak is the cloth of the T'boli people who live in the highlands of South Cotabato. Fiber from abaca, a banana species native to the Philippines (also called Manila hemp), is spun into thread, sections of the thread are bound with a resist material such as wax and dyed in the ikat technique so the pattern is set in advance, and the thread is then woven on a backstrap loom. What makes the cloth special is the belief that its designs come from dreams. A T'boli woman dreams that Fu Dalu, the goddess of abaca, shows her a pattern, and after waking she weaves exactly what she saw. That is why the weavers are called dreamweavers. Because the designs come from dreams, they cannot be mass-produced like factory prints, which adds to the value of the cloth.

The main place to meet T'nalak is the Lang Dulay Weaving Center in the Lamdalag area near Lake Sebu. Its original name is the Manlilikha ng Bayan Center, a workshop set up in her hometown by Lang Dulay (1928–2015), a T'nalak master weaver who received the Gawad sa Manlilikha ng Bayan (GAMABA), the National Living Treasures Award. Several travel accounts say that on the second floor of a traditional T'boli house you can watch women weavers set up their threads at the looms without making an appointment. On the Lake Sebu town side there is also the School of Living Traditions, where weaver Barbara Ofong volunteers, and where you can experience T'boli dance, music and homestays alongside weaving.

Keep in mind that this is a working workshop, not a tourist showroom. Watching a weaver at the loom and taking photos is welcome, but rushing or haggling constantly can make the atmosphere awkward. Weaving one piece takes several months. Sources vary from 2 to 6 months, depending on the complexity of the pattern and the weaver. Knowing this makes a higher price easier to understand. This guide covers the background of T'nalak, how to visit, how to buy, and how to get there from Manila, centered on the weaving center and the School of Living Traditions.

A T'nalak design also appears on Philippine banknotes. It is on the reverse of the 1,000-peso note in the New Generation Currency Series, so checking the bills in your wallet before you go is a nice bit of preparation. Note that older blogs and newer news articles give different figures for transport and prices. The prices and times here are approximate, drawn from sources dated 2012 to 2025, so please confirm the latest information locally.

Weavers work T'nalak on backstrap looms in a second-floor workshop in a traditional T'boli house. One travel account says there is no entrance fee but donations are expected, and you can buy finished cloth directly from the weavers. A few meters from the center there is also a T'nalak gallery curated by an NCCA commissioner, where you can compare many designs.

The designs said to be shown by the goddess Fu Dalu carry names such as bulinglangit (clouds), bankiring (hair bangs) and kabangi (butterfly). Lang Dulay is said to have remembered more than 100 designs.

T'nalak uses only three colors: white, red and black. White is the natural abaca color and stands for purity. Red comes from the roots of the loko tree and stands for blood. Black comes from boiling the leaves of the knalum tree for a long time and stands for soil. The background is mostly black, with white motifs and red accents.

The school in Lake Sebu town is a T'boli homestay in a traditional house where village children learn traditional arts on weekends. Visitors can meet weavers and watch T'boli dance and music. It is safest to contact them before visiting to confirm the schedule.

Lang Dulay was named a National Living Treasure in 1998, and in 2023 Lake Sebu produced three more: Barbara Ofong (T'nalak weaving), Rosie Sula (T'boli chanting) and Bundos Fara (temwel brass casting). Few places gather so many living treasures in one community.

T'nalak was used at major life events such as birth, marriage and death. It was a prized possession at weddings, and it is said it was also used as a covering during childbirth to help ensure a safe delivery. It is believed that cutting the cloth brings sickness, so it is not cut, and when it is sold a brass ring is said to be placed around it to please the spirits.

The former T'boli Museum in Lake Sebu town opened in 1988 and is now called the House of Gongs. It holds gongs dating back to the 17th century, 15th-century Ming Dynasty porcelain plates, and instruments such as the kulintang, so it pairs well with a weaving visit.

South Cotabato holds the T'nalak Festival every year on July 18, the anniversary of the founding of the province. It is a province-wide event, and its name comes from the cloth, which suits a trip to the weaving villages.
From Lake Sebu town, take a motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) to the Lang Dulay Weaving Center in Lamdalag. On the map it is about
3km
from the town center. Check the fare with the driver first.
Watch a weaver at the backstrap loom in the second-floor workshop. They are working, so greet them before speaking, and ask permission before taking photos.
At the nearby T'nalak gallery, compare designs such as clouds, butterflies and shields. Each design has a name and a story, and it is much more fun with an explanation.
If you like a cloth, buy it directly from the weaver. One account says a roll is about
7m
and the shortest piece sold was
, so ask about length first. Bring cash.
Return to town for lunch at a restaurant that serves the area's well-known fried tilapia (chicharong tilapia).
In the afternoon you can continue to Seven Falls or the House of Gongs. These times are only suggestions, and the center's opening hours are hard to confirm officially, so check locally.

items.title: Overnight route
items.subtitle: Homestay at the School of Living Traditions

children.text: Take a van from General Santos to Lake Sebu and check in at the School of Living Traditions (SLT). It helps to ask the driver to drop you in front of the school.
Greet the weavers in the school's traditional house and listen to stories about T'nalak.
Watch T'boli music and dance performed by the host family. Travel accounts mention dances such as Madal Mit Mata and Madal Ewas.
In the morning, see the lotus flowers near the lake (the flowers are said to close soon after sunrise) and rent a traditional costume for photos.
Go to the Lang Dulay Weaving Center, look around the workshop and buy souvenirs.
Fly from Manila to General Santos (GES). Airlines, frequencies and flight times change with the season, so check the latest schedule on a booking site.
General Santos is the nearest airport to the South Cotabato area, and all the travel accounts describe this route.
From the airport to the van terminal in the city, take a taxi or a multicab.

If you go by bus, another route described goes from Koronadal to Surallah, then by van or jeepney to Lake Sebu.

items.title: From town to the weaving center

children.text: In Lake Sebu town, the motorcycle taxi (habal-habal) is almost the only way to get around. One record gives a minimum fare of about
for a short trip, and you should agree on the fare to the weaving center with the driver first.
You register your names at the terminal and pay according to the posted rate list, so check the list.
T'nalak weaving can be seen all year, but one travel account says abaca fiber breaks easily in hot weather, so weavers work when it is cool. The lake surface is at about
above sea level, so the highlands are relatively cool and watching the weaving is comfortable.

South Cotabato is known to have no pronounced dry or wet season and almost no typhoons. Still, rain can make motorcycle taxis and waterfall visits uncomfortable, so check the weather before you go. To overlap with a festival, aim for the T'nalak Festival around July 18 or the Helobung Festival on November 11.

There are two kinds of lodging. One is the homestay at the School of Living Traditions (SLT): a 2020 travel account lists a fan room at about ₱350 per person with breakfast, and says backpacker space is used when no rooms are free. You sleep in the gono bong, the big room of a T'boli house, in a bed with cloth sides called a klabo. The other is the Lemobung Tourism Lodge, which the same account lists at about ₱100 per person, but there are no restaurants nearby so you need to buy food in advance. All of these rates are old, so confirm before booking.

The signature food is tilapia from the lake. A plate of crispy fried tilapia is about ₱250–350 and can be shared by 3–5 people, according to one record. There do not seem to be many restaurants around the weaving center, so have lunch in town.
The center is a working workshop, so watch quietly and ask permission before photographing the weavers.
Bring plenty of cash. Buying directly from the weavers is easiest with cash.
T'nalak is described as a sacred cloth. It may be used as an accent on Filipiniana attire but not as bedding, so do not treat its use lightly.
There is a tradition that cutting the cloth brings sickness, so ask about lengths respectfully.
Prices on older blogs are more than ten years old. Ask the weaver for the current price first rather than haggling.
The last direct van from General Santos is recorded at around 4–5 PM in 2020 but at 3 PM in a 2024 guide, so arrive at the terminal before 3 PM and avoid arriving late.
Contact the School of Living Traditions before visiting to confirm the schedule. One travel account says a class was canceled when the instructor was away.
The order recommended in travel accounts is to see the lake's lotus flowers early in the morning, then tour the weaving center and waterfalls during the day.
Opening hours, booking methods and fees at the weaving center and the school are hard to confirm officially. Contact the local tourism office or the school before you leave.
Many of the prices and transport details here are based on 2012–2020 travel accounts. Check the latest notices.
Weavers do not always receive visitors. A weaver may be away or there may be no work that day.
Agree on the motorcycle taxi fare before riding, and ask for a helmet because the roads can be slippery in the rain.
You are visiting an indigenous community, so follow local etiquette on photos, dress and touching items.
The lake town where the weaving center is. The lake, Seven Falls and the lotus flowers are close, and you get around by motorcycle taxi.
A former T'boli museum built in 1988 with gongs, kulintang and Ming porcelain. It is in the Poblacion of the town.
Lake Sebu's best-known group of waterfalls, with a zipline. Some falls need a 20–30 minute walk down.
A small waterfall with a reported entrance fee of about ₱20. Bring a change of clothes.
